title: The stranger, the widow, the orphan (Exodus 22:21–27)
hook: you were strangers in Egypt; if he cries to me, I will hear

segments.voice: Yesterday, the second half of the ten words, lo tirtzach among them, ending with the one about wanting. Your line was ten words for living.

It's your first week in a new country. You don't know which line to stand in. You can't read the forms. Someone at a counter speaks to you slowly and loudly, as if you were a child, and the people behind you sigh. You smile, because you need what's at the end of that line. A new school, a new job, a hospital in another city can give a small taste of it. Right after the ten words, Exodus starts filling in what they look like on the ground, and soon the law turns to exactly that person: the one who doesn't belong yet.
screen: `YOUR FIRST WEEK IN A NEW COUNTRY.` → `THE WRONG LINE, THE WRONG FORM.` → `THE LAW TURNS TO THAT PERSON.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "Thou shalt neither vex a stranger, nor oppress him: for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt." The Hebrew word for stranger is ger: someone living among a people who isn't one of them. Not a tourist. A neighbor without roots, without land, without family to stand up for him. And notice the reason. Not politeness. Memory. You were the ones in the wrong line once. A chapter later the law says it more tenderly: "ye know the heart of a stranger, seeing ye were strangers in the land of Egypt." Then the circle widens. "Ye shall not afflict any widow, or fatherless child." In the world of the text, a widow or an orphan could easily be left with no one to speak for them, and nothing to stop them being pushed aside. And here God steps in personally: if you afflict them and they cry to me, I will surely hear their cry. Then the law gets very small and practical. If you lend to a poor neighbor, don't charge interest. If you take his cloak as a pledge, give it back before the sun goes down, because "that is his covering only," and wherein shall he sleep? God's reason: "when he crieth unto me, that I will hear; for I am gracious." Some Christians hear an echo in Matthew's Gospel, where Jesus says, "I was a stranger, and ye took me in." The stranger, the widow, the orphan: three people with no one else to stand up for them.
screen: `GER: SOMEONE WITHOUT ROOTS.` · `YOU KNOW THE HEART OF A STRANGER.` · `THE WIDOW AND THE ORPHAN.` · `GIVE BACK THE CLOAK BY SUNDOWN.` · then, large: `FOR YE WERE STRANGERS IN THE LAND OF EGYPT.`

segments.voice: Remember a time you were the stranger, new, lost, unsure where to stand, and feel it again for a moment. Then think of someone who's there now, a new coworker, a family who just moved in, someone grieving, and one small thing you could give: food, money, time, a name remembered. If you pray, you can hold them in prayer.
The stranger. In Hebrew, ger: someone living among you without land or family. The law protects him because Israel remembers being one.
Your line: you were strangers too. Memory can make a heart kind. Day three hundred ninety-six, done.

howItsDone: Some churches run food pantries, refugee resettlement programs and ministries to widows and orphans, and some Christians cite Exodus 22 and Matthew 25 together when explaining why.

chat.says: Why does Exodus keep telling Israel to be kind to strangers?
options: Because they remember: they were strangers in Egypt, so they know a stranger's heart.
Because strangers paid taxes to the king, so mistreating them hurt the nation.
Because strangers were usually rich traders who could repay the favor later.
chat.meaning: The law gives a reason from memory: ye were strangers in the land of Egypt, and ye know the heart of a stranger.

ger.meaning: Hebrew for a stranger living among another people

fatherless.meaning: orphaned, with no father to protect them

pledge.meaning: something held as a promise that a loan will be repaid
